questions: Does the oval still finish 20/20 near 1.65 s with the shorter body (lower yaw inertia), or does the controller now overshoot on the oval?
On the s-bend and slalom, does progress rise above 0.17 and 0.12, and at what lateral error does the first line loss occur?
Does steering oscillation fall or rise relative to the baseline's 0.15 on the oval? A rise would suggest yaw inertia was helping damp the controller.

intent: Single-variable test against the iteration-0 baseline: reduce body_length from 0.16 m to 0.12 m, cutting yaw inertia by about 25 percent, and keep every other value identical. Expected: the oval stays at 20/20 near 1.65 s, and s-bend and slalom progress rises above 0.17 and 0.12. If the oval falls, the baseline body length stays the reference for the final design.
learning: Iterations 1 to 7 show that the controller-geometry pair is tuned to the baseline. Lead, footprint, spread, track, radius and mass each collapse or degrade the oval when changed. The wider array's apparent bend benefit was not reproduced with a stable drivetrain, so spread is not the bend lever. Body length (yaw inertia) is the last untested geometry lever. If it also fails, the bend limit is controller-side (gains or base speed), and the final geometry should be the baseline.
rationale: Race evidence: the iteration-0 baseline (0.6 kg, 0.12 m track, 0.03 m radius, five sensors at x = ±0.024 m on a 12 mm pitch, y = 0.05 m, 12 mm footprint) is still the best design at 356.6. It finishes the oval 20/20 in about 1.65 s but leaves the track on the s-bend (progress 0.17) and slalom (progress 0.12). Every deviation since has hurt the oval. Lead at y = 0.03 m and y = 0.07 m each collapsed it to 0/20, and so did footprints of 8 mm and 16 mm. Iteration 7 corrects an earlier reading: the wider ±0.032 m array with the baseline 0.6 kg drivetrain also collapsed the oval to 0/20 and did not improve the bends (s-bend 0.168, slalom 0.125, both no better than baseline). So the iteration-2 bend gain was not a real spread effect, and I drop the spread hypothesis. Levers already tested: spread, lead, footprint, track, radius, and mass (in combination). Body length has not been tested. Body width is not a lever: with the 0.0125 m tape half-width, the off-track limit only exceeds the 0.06 m floor when body_width exceeds about 0.19 m, which is out of range. Body length changes only yaw inertia, mass*(L² + W²)/12. Going from L = 0.16 to 0.12 m with W = 0.14 m and 0.6 kg cuts yaw inertia by about 25 percent (0.0452 to 0.0340 in the bracket), and does not touch sensing or drivetrain. That is the cleanest single-variable test left. Decision: keep the sensor array, lead, footprint, drivetrain and mass exactly as baseline, and change only body_length from 0.16 to 0.12 m. Expected result: the oval still finishes near 20/20 at about 1.65 s, with equal or lower steering oscillation, and bend progress rises slightly, perhaps to 0.2 or more. If the oval drops below baseline finish rate, body yaw inertia is confirmed as the controller-sensitive axis and the baseline should be the final geometry. Uncertainty is high: the controller appears tuned to the baseline, so any geometry change may break it.
